input.question: Why are the tides in the Bay of Fundy so much more extreme?
input.ground_truth: The short version is that the Minas Basin in the Bay of Fundy gets narrower so as the mass of water gets pulled into the bay, the water gets forced together and the tide gets higher. The longer answer is that the number of tides per day (0, 2 or 4 are the most common), their relative heights (all equal, or major and minor), and their absolute heights are a result of how water flows around the land masses. Obviously the relative position of the sun and moon, and how close they are to perihelion can will also have an effect, but that tends to affect the entire planet equally. There aren't even hard rules that east or west facing bays have higher tides since further north the Leaf Basin in Ungava Bay faces the other direction but has tides that are approximately as high. Wikipeadia has a [diagram](_URL_0_) showing the heights of tides which might help explain how the water moves.
